name: Hassan Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining companies or technology firms, and what you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a haul-truck crew and use the mine's approved voice assistant to read long service notes while I am wearing gloves. I check its wording against the laminated maintenance sheet before telling the next driver what needs attention.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you engaged in the work, and what is difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing a small snag before it delays the whole pit. My pay is high and I have about eight months of expenses saved, so I can take time to test an idea instead of jumping at a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a little time saved on notes is useful if it does not erase a warning. I will still have a driver confirm the route before a loaded truck moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my paid day is operating equipment, and this picture says jobs and pay carry on much as before. I do not expect my own hours to change from a small routine tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my regular rotation and use the assistant for long notes after checking the printed sheet. I would keep my normal saving transfer rather than buy another device for a problem the mine has not shown me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my work and income in this mild version. I am curious about the time saved, but I would not change a route routine that keeps the crew out of trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check whether the assistant had missed something important?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare a week of spoken notes with the signed maintenance sheet and ask the mechanic about each difference. If it dropped a brake or tire warning, I would stop using it for that kind of note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the other operators to use it too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let one experienced driver try it on a day shift first. If the spoken version stayed accurate and made handover easier, I would show the rest of the crew how to check it.

say: I would welcome small savings if **warnings stay visible**.
I will have a driver confirm **the route** before a loaded truck moves.
think: I think my paid shift remains **mostly hands-on**.
I do not expect a routine tool to **cut my hours**.
do: Keep my **regular rotation** and check spoken notes against the printed sheet.
Continue my **normal savings transfer** instead of buying new gear.
feel: I feel **calm** about my work and income in this mild version.
S0.quote: I will still have a driver confirm the route before a loaded truck moves.
fieldNote: Hassan uses voice tools but checks **maintenance warnings** against a signed sheet.
His higher pay and **strong savings** make the mild case financially secure.
He prefers a **one-shift test** before extending the tool to the crew.

steps.text: Keep the regular rotation and check voice notes against the printed sheet
Compare spoken notes with the mechanic's signed service sheet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the planner needs to show what it changed, not just give a new line. A map can be outdated, but the driver can see changes on the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already use one approved tool for service notes, so I can learn a planner if another crew proves it useful. I am uneasy that my lead hours could shrink while operators are asked to check more software output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its route choices with the haul-road board for two weeks, then ask a day-shift lead to review the results. If the tool were accurate, I would learn the planning feature on paid time and keep the paper board beside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the route and booking work may change before the truck work does. I would check my lead allowance and overtime instead of assuming software saves money by removing the whole crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you that your own duties or pay had changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the rota and allowance on two pay slips before and after the planner starts. If the lead hours fell, I would ask the superintendent to show the new staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the planner conflicts with a road closure, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the test and check the closure with the radio operator. I would report the mismatch and use the signed road notice until the system team corrected it.

say: I would ask the planner to explain **what it changed**.
I would keep a **paper map** for the road check.
think: I can learn a planner after another crew **proves it useful**.
I worry my lead hours could shrink while **review work grows**.
do: Compare planner choices with the **haul-road board** for two weeks.
Learn the feature on paid time and keep **paper checks** beside it.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about changing lead work, not an immediate truck cut.
S1.quote: A map can be outdated, but the driver can see changes on the road.
fieldNote: Hassan is a **proven-use adopter**, not an automatic tech enthusiast.
He worries about lead hours if software adds **unpaid review work**.
He checks output against road boards and **closure notices**.

steps.text: Compare planner choices with the haul-road board for two weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would explain that thinking AI arrives first and robots for hands-on work follow about three years later. I would ask the mine for funded training places and real job numbers, because a quick announcement does not tell a crew where to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my truck hours could fall by 2031, even if the first changes are in planning and paperwork. Eight months saved and several mines nearby give me some control, but I would not leave a high-paying job for a course with no employer behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the mine to fund a physical equipment-inspection course, and I would enroll if the employer paid and a mechanic confirmed it taught hands-on checks. In 2029, after AGI arrives, I would apply for inspection work only if the job involved hands-on checks and the wage was written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because robots could replace the main task I am paid for within five years. My savings and nearby jobs give me choices, but I still need to start before several crews are looking for work at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection role is mainly records or diagnosis that AGI can do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would not treat it as protected work, because AGI can do those thinking tasks too. I would ask whether a worker still inspects the physical equipment and how many paid posts the mine expects after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mine cannot state the pay or duration, what would you do in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current job and compare other mines before spending on a course. I would move only for a written job with a wage that fits the bills.

fieldNote: Hassan expects **robot exposure** to threaten his main task by 2031.
He has options but will not self-fund a course without an **employer**.
He distinguishes physical inspection from **AGI-suited records and diagnosis**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives people time to learn another trade if the mine pays for training. I would also ask the company to publish how many physical jobs it expects to keep after 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight years gives me time to learn physical inspection while I keep my truck wage. AGI can do records and diagnosis, so I would need to know whether any hands-on inspection posts remain after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would finish a paid equipment-inspection course before 2031 and keep my truck qualification current. In 2032, the first year after AGI arrives, I would apply for physical inspection work only if the wage and expected duration were clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because I can prepare, but the mine has not promised how many jobs remain. I would keep earning while I train rather than leave my current crew for a short contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you pay for further training after that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask nearby mines whether the certificate leads to physical inspection shifts and what those workers earn. If the work were mostly records or diagnosis, I would not spend more because AGI can do that part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2032, if inspection work looks temporary before robots arrive, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a role if the pay covered my costs and gave me time to look for the next job before 2034. If the contract did not, I would stay with my current crew and keep checking openings.

say: I would say five years gives people time to **learn another trade**.
I would ask for job numbers after **2034**.
think: Eight years lets me train while **keeping my truck wage**.
I need to know if hands-on posts remain after **robots arrive**.
do: Finish the paid **equipment-inspection course** before 2031 and keep my qualification current.
In 2032, apply only with clear **wage and duration**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because I can prepare, but hiring is unknown.
S3.quote: Eight years gives me time to learn physical inspection while I keep my truck wage.
fieldNote: Hassan sees the longer timeline as **room to train** while earning.
He rules out records and diagnosis as a safe **post-AGI career**.
He checks physical **vacancies and terms** before moving.

steps.text: Finish the paid equipment-inspection course before 2031
Apply for physical inspection work with clear pay in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mine to publish its training routes and expected job numbers well before 2036. I would say the robot lag gives workers time, but nobody should call that a guarantee of future work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years before robots arrive gives me time to build options while earning a strong wage. I would still check whether physical inspection work lasts after 2039 before I put years into that trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current job and review which paid courses have led to physical jobs at nearby mines. In 2037, the first year after AGI arrives, I would compare vacancies and wages before deciding whether to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because my income and savings give me years to prepare. I would not leave a good role before an employer showed me the work, the pay and how long it was expected to last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to know before accepting an inspection role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask what parts of the job are physical, what it pays and whether the work continues after 2039. I would also check whether the course qualifies me at more than one mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the job forecasts are uncertain in 2037, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep earning in my current role and ask other mines for updated numbers. I would wait for a written vacancy and wage before making a move.

say: I would ask for **training routes** and job numbers before 2036.
I would not call the robot lag a **work guarantee**.
think: I have thirteen years to build options while **earning a strong wage**.
I will check if inspection lasts after **2039**.
do: Review paid courses that lead to **physical jobs**.
In 2037, compare vacancies and **wages at nearby mines** before moving.
feel: I feel **calm** because my income and savings give me years to prepare.
S4.quote: Thirteen years before robots arrive gives me time to build options while earning a strong wage.
fieldNote: Hassan treats the long lead as **time to prepare**, not a guarantee.
He wants course outcomes and **job forecasts** before committing.
His income and savings mean there is no need for a **rushed move**.

steps.text: Keep the current role while reviewing course outcomes at nearby mines

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could affect my main task by around 2031. Paid training, actual job numbers and a clear wage would help me choose a next step without rushing out of a good role.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want any new machine to be judged by the work it actually does. If it helps with notes, fine, but the driver still needs authority to stop when the road is unsafe.

headlineQuote: I want any new machine to be judged by the work it actually does.
portrait: Hassan Rahman is **27** and leads a haul-truck crew at a large mine.
He earns **higher pay** and has more than six months of expenses saved.
Plenty of similar mines nearby give him **options** if his role changes.
He uses an **approved voice assistant** daily and checks it against maintenance sheets.
He is willing to retrain after seeing clear job numbers and **wages**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves about five years before robots could reduce his truck hours.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, actual job numbers and a clear wage would help Hassan choose a next step.
